claims.claim: The National Flood Insurance Act of 1968 created the NFIP, whose twin purposes were sharing flood risk through insurance and reducing damages by restricting floodplain development.
claims.episode_span: The National Flood Insurance Act of 1968 created a federal program that would sell policies at rates intended to reflect risk
claims.supporting_quote: The NFIP has two purposes: to share the risk of flood losses through flood insurance and to reduce flood damages by restricting floodplain development

claims.claim: Geographer Gilbert White, often called the father of floodplain management, shaped the intellectual basis of U.S. flood policy.
claims.episode_span: Policymakers, drawing on work by geographer Gilbert White and others
claims.supporting_quote: was a prominent American geographer , sometimes termed the "father of floodplain management"

claims.claim: The Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973 made flood insurance purchase mandatory for property in Special Flood Hazard Areas (tied to federally backed mortgages).
claims.episode_span: accelerated after major floods in the 1970s prompted Congress to make coverage mandatory for mortgaged properties in participating areas
claims.supporting_quote: The program was first amended by the Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973, which made the purchase of flood insurance mandatory for the protection of property within SFHAs

claims.claim: The NFIP was premium-funded until the end of 2004, after which it borrowed heavily, primarily because of Hurricanes Katrina and Sandy.
claims.episode_span: When Hurricane Katrina struck in 2005, the NFIP faced claims that pushed the program more than $17 billion into debt
claims.supporting_quote: The cost of the insurance program was fully covered by its premiums until the end of 2004, but it has had to steadily borrow funds since, primarily due to Hurricane Katrina and Hurricane Sandy , accumulating $25 billion of debt by August 2017

claims.claim: The NFIP's cumulative debt exceeded $17 billion by the end of 2011 (post-Katrina), when Congress passed Biggert-Waters.
claims.episode_span: claims that pushed the program more than $17 billion into debt
claims.supporting_quote: At the conclusion of 2011, as Congress passed Biggert-Waters, the NFIP cumulative debt was over $17 billion

claims.claim: The Biggert-Waters Flood Insurance Reform Act of 2012 moved NFIP premiums toward actuarial risk-based rates, removing discounts and grandfathering.
claims.episode_span: The Biggert-Waters Flood Insurance Reform Act of 2012 directed FEMA to phase out many subsidies
claims.supporting_quote: A core principle of Biggert-Waters was to change the NFIP premiums to match actuarial risk-based premiums that better reflected the expected losses and real risk of flooding

claims.claim: In March 2014 President Obama signed the Homeowner Flood Insurance Affordability Act, which reinstated grandfathered lower rates and delayed Biggert-Waters premium increases.
claims.episode_span: In 2014 Congress passed the Homeowner Flood Insurance Affordability Act, which restored many of the discounts and slowed the transition to risk-based rates
claims.supporting_quote: In March 2014, President Obama signed the Homeowner Flood Insurance Affordability Act of 2013 . The bill changed the process used to alter subsidized premiums and reinstated grandfathering of lower rates

claims.claim: Repetitive-loss properties cost the NFIP about $200 million annually (GAO, 2003).
claims.episode_span: a class of repetitive-loss properties emerged—structures that filed multiple claims yet remained in place
claims.supporting_quote: In 2003, the GAO found that repetitive-loss properties cost the program about $200 million annually

claims.claim: Flood insurance administration moved from HUD to FEMA when FEMA was created in 1979 and absorbed the Federal Insurance Administration.
claims.episode_span: The program began operations in 1969 under the Department of Housing and Urban Development and later moved to the Federal Emergency Management Agency
claims.supporting_quote: FEMA absorbed the Federal Insurance Administration , the National Fire Prevention and Control Administration

claims.claim: Overconfidence in levees and other structural flood works encourages building on floodplains and produces worse disasters when defenses are breached (Gilbert White's central finding).
claims.episode_span: the combination of affordable premiums and the visible presence of levees produced the opposite result
claims.supporting_quote: Public confidence in structural works increased occupance of, and building on floodplains. Design standards are sometimes inappropriate, and overconfidence develops, resulting in worse disasters if a flood breaches defenses
